claims.text: The Aztecs used cacao beans as small change in their markets.
The Aztecs did not use maize kernels, coffee beans or chilli seeds as money; coffee was unknown in the Americas then.
Aztec cotton cloaks, called quachtli, served as money for larger sums.
Spanish chroniclers reported counterfeit cacao beans made by filling empty shells with earth.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Counterfeiters emptied real beans and refilled them with mud or sand, and also made fakes from ash, clay, amaranth dough, wax, or avocado pits. The search did not surface the chroniclers' own writings, so I can't confirm their specific accounts of counterfeiting.

claimResults.note: The search supports the method: counterfeiters emptied real beans and refilled them with mud or sand, and also made fakes of clay, wax or amaranth dough. It did not surface any chronicler's account, so 'Spanish chroniclers reported' is unverified here. I recall Sahagun and Oviedo describing forged beans, but not well enough to call it certain.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: The search did not find any source that attributes the counterfeit-bean description to Oviedo or Sahagún. The claim appears in modern sources without a named chronicler. The counterfeiting itself is well documented in modern summaries. One Penn Museum article says counterfeit "coins" were created by filling empty cacao shells with clay or sand. Wikipedia's Aztec cuisine article says beans were frequently counterfeited by filling empty cacao shells with dirt or mud. Oviedo does not appear in any result.

claimResults.note: The forgery itself is confirmed (the Penn Museum: empty cacao shells filled with clay or sand; Wikipedia: with dirt or mud), but no result attributes the report to a Spanish chronicler: the summary says the claim appears in modern sources without a named chronicler, and neither Sahagun's nor Oviedo's text was retrieved. So 'Spanish chroniclers reported' stays unconfirmed.

issues.note: Checker doubt on c4: the attribution to Spanish chroniclers has no Tier A or B support. Checker B's rewording fits the evidence: 'Forgers made fake beans by filling empty shells with earth' (the Penn Museum says clay or sand, Wikipedia dirt or mud).
